claim: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and the Linear Mixed-effects Model (LMM), sometimes in combination, are the most common genetic association models.
source: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and the Linear Mixed-effects Model (LMM), sometimes in combination, are the most common genetic association models.
evidence: This is a statement of established practice in the field, drawing from general scientific knowledge about genetic association methods.

claim: Previous PCA-LMM comparisons give mixed results, unclear guidance, and have several limitations, including not varying the number of principal components (PCs), simulating simple population structures, and inconsistent use of real data and power evaluations.
source: Previous PCA-LMM comparisons give mixed results, unclear guidance, and have several limitations, including not varying the number of principal components (PCs), simulating simple population structures, and inconsistent use of real data and power evaluations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the literature review presented in Table 1 and the discussion of previous studies throughout the introduction.

claim: LMM without PCs usually performs best, with the largest effects in family simulations and real human datasets and traits without environment effects.
source: We find that LMM without PCs usually performs best, with the largest effects in family simulations and real human datasets and traits without environment effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented in Table 3, Figures 3-5, and the statistical analyses throughout the Results section.

claim: Poor PCA performance on human datasets is driven by large numbers of distant relatives more than the smaller number of closer relatives.
source: Poor PCA performance on human datasets is driven by large numbers of distant relatives more than the smaller number of closer relatives.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of local kinship (Figure 6) and the evaluation after removing 4th degree relatives (Figure 7, Table 4).

claim: PCA was known to fail on family data.
source: While PCA was known to fail on family data, we report strong effects of family relatedness in genetically diverse human datasets, not avoided by pruning close relatives.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Patterson et al., 2006; Zhu and Yu, 2009; Thornton and McPeek, 2010; Price et al., 2010) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: Strong effects of family relatedness occur in genetically diverse human datasets, not avoided by pruning close relatives.
source: While PCA was known to fail on family data, we report strong effects of family relatedness in genetically diverse human datasets, not avoided by pruning close relatives.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results showing poor PCA performance even after removing 4th degree relatives (Figure 7, Table 4).

claim: Environment effects driven by geography and ethnicity are better modeled with LMM including those labels instead of PCs.
source: Environment effects driven by geography and ethnicity are better modeled with LMM including those labels instead of PCs.
evidence: This is supported by the environment simulation results showing that 'LMM lab.' (with true group labels) substantially outperforms both PCA and LMM with PCs (Figure 8, Table 6).

claim: Association studies of admixed and multiethnic cohorts are becoming more common.
source: Association studies of admixed and multiethnic cohorts, the focus of this work, are becoming more common, are believed to be more powerful, and are necessary to bring more equity to genetic medicine (Rosenberg et al., 2010; Hoffman and Dubé, 2013; Coram et al., 2013; Medina-Gomez et al., 2015; Conomos et al., 2016a; Hodonsky et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017a; Martin et al., 2017b; Hindorff et al., 2018; Hoffmann et al., 2018; Mogil et al., 2018; Roselli et al., 2018; Wojcik et al., 2019; Peterson et al., 2019; Zhong et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2020; Simonin-Wilmer et al., 2021; Kamariza et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2021; Mahajan et al., 2022; Hou et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Association studies of admixed and multiethnic cohorts are believed to be more powerful.
source: Association studies of admixed and multiethnic cohorts, the focus of this work, are becoming more common, are believed to be more powerful, and are necessary to bring more equity to genetic medicine (Rosenberg et al., 2010; Hoffman and Dubé, 2013; Coram et al., 2013; Medina-Gomez et al., 2015; Conomos et al., 2016a; Hodonsky et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017a; Martin et al., 2017b; Hindorff et al., 2018; Hoffmann et al., 2018; Mogil et al., 2018; Roselli et al., 2018; Wojcik et al., 2019; Peterson et al., 2019; Zhong et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2020; Simonin-Wilmer et al., 2021; Kamariza et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2021; Mahajan et al., 2022; Hou et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature discussing the benefits of diverse cohorts.

claim: Association studies of admixed and multiethnic cohorts are necessary to bring more equity to genetic medicine.
source: Association studies of admixed and multiethnic cohorts, the focus of this work, are becoming more common, are believed to be more powerful, and are necessary to bring more equity to genetic medicine (Rosenberg et al., 2010; Hoffman and Dubé, 2013; Coram et al., 2013; Medina-Gomez et al., 2015; Conomos et al., 2016a; Hodonsky et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017a; Martin et al., 2017b; Hindorff et al., 2018; Hoffmann et al., 2018; Mogil et al., 2018; Roselli et al., 2018; Wojcik et al., 2019; Peterson et al., 2019; Zhong et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2020; Simonin-Wilmer et al., 2021; Kamariza et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2021; Mahajan et al., 2022; Hou et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on equity in genetic medicine.

claim: When insufficient approaches are applied to data with relatedness, their association statistics are miscalibrated, resulting in excess false positives and loss of power.
source: When insufficient approaches are applied to data with relatedness, their association statistics are miscalibrated, resulting in excess false positives and loss of power (Devlin and Roeder, 1999; Voight and Pritchard, 2005; Astle and Balding, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work demonstrating the consequences of inadequate modeling of relatedness.

claim: Genetic association with PCA consists of including the top eigenvectors of the population kinship matrix as covariates in a generalized linear model.
source: Genetic association with PCA consists of including the top eigenvectors of the population kinship matrix as covariates in a generalized linear model (Zhang et al., 2003; Price et al., 2006; Bouaziz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citations to foundational papers.

claim: PCs map to ancestry empirically.
source: These models are deeply connected because PCs map to ancestry empirically (Alexander et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2016) and theoretically (McVean, 2009; Zheng and Weir, 2016; Cabreros and Storey, 2019; Chiu et al., 2022), and they work as well as global ancestry in association studies but are estimated more easily (Patterson et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2007; Alexander et al., 2009; Bouaziz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: PCs map to ancestry theoretically.
source: These models are deeply connected because PCs map to ancestry empirically (Alexander et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2016) and theoretically (McVean, 2009; Zheng and Weir, 2016; Cabreros and Storey, 2019; Chiu et al., 2022), and they work as well as global ancestry in association studies but are estimated more easily (Patterson et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2007; Alexander et al., 2009; Bouaziz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: PCs work as well as global ancestry in association studies but are estimated more easily.
source: These models are deeply connected because PCs map to ancestry empirically (Alexander et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2016) and theoretically (McVean, 2009; Zheng and Weir, 2016; Cabreros and Storey, 2019; Chiu et al., 2022), and they work as well as global ancestry in association studies but are estimated more easily (Patterson et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2007; Alexander et al., 2009; Bouaziz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: PCA assumes that the underlying relatedness space is low dimensional (or low rank).
source: However, PCA assumes that the underlying relatedness space is low dimensional (or low rank), so it can be well modeled with a small number of PCs, which may limit its applicability.
evidence: This is an inference about the mathematical properties of PCA based on established knowledge of the method.

claim: PCA is known to be inadequate for family data.
source: PCA is known to be inadequate for family data (Patterson et al., 2006; Zhu and Yu, 2009; Thornton and McPeek, 2010; Price et al., 2010), which is called 'cryptic relatedness' when it is unknown to the researchers, but no other troublesome cases have been confidently identified.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work demonstrating PCA's limitations with family data.

claim: LMM includes a random effect parameterized by the kinship matrix.
source: The other dominant association model under relatedness is the LMM, which includes a random effect parameterized by the kinship matrix.
evidence: This is a methodological description based on established knowledge of LMMs.

claim: Unlike PCA, LMM does not assume that relatedness is low-dimensional.
source: Unlike PCA, LMM does not assume that relatedness is low-dimensional, and explicitly models families via the kinship matrix.
evidence: This is an inference about the mathematical properties of LMM compared to PCA.

claim: LMM explicitly models families via the kinship matrix.
source: Unlike PCA, LMM does not assume that relatedness is low-dimensional, and explicitly models families via the kinship matrix.
evidence: This is a methodological description based on established knowledge of LMMs.

claim: Modern LMMs estimate kinship from genotypes using a non-parametric estimator that captures the combined covariance due to family relatedness and ancestry.
source: Modern LMMs estimate kinship from genotypes using a non-parametric estimator, often referred to as a genetic relationship matrix, that captures the combined covariance due to family relatedness and ancestry (Kang et al., 2008; Astle and Balding, 2009; Ochoa and Storey, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological papers.

claim: Some previous work has found the apparent redundancy of an LMM with PCs beneficial.
source: However, some previous work has found the apparent redundancy of an LMM with PCs beneficial (Price et al., 2010; Tucker et al., 2014; Zhang and Pan, 2015), while others did not (Liu et al., 2011; Janss et al., 2012), and the approach continues to be used (Zeng et al., 2018; Mbatchou et al., 2021), although not always (Matoba et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies with mixed findings.

claim: Some previous work did not find the apparent redundancy of an LMM with PCs beneficial.
source: However, some previous work has found the apparent redundancy of an LMM with PCs beneficial (Price et al., 2010; Tucker et al., 2014; Zhang and Pan, 2015), while others did not (Liu et al., 2011; Janss et al., 2012), and the approach continues to be used (Zeng et al., 2018; Mbatchou et al., 2021), although not always (Matoba et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies with mixed findings.

claim: Direct comparisons between LMM and PCA have yielded mixed results.
source: Direct comparisons have yielded mixed results, with several studies finding superior performance for LMM, notably from papers promoting advances in LMMs, while many others report comparable performance (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the literature review presented in Table 1.

claim: No papers find that PCA outperforms LMM decisively.
source: No papers find that PCA outperforms LMM decisively, although PCA occasionally performs better in isolated and artificial cases or individual measures, often with unknown significance.
evidence: This is an inference from the literature review presented in Table 1.

claim: Previous studies generally used either only simulated or only real genotypes, with only two studies using both.
source: Previous studies generally used either only simulated or only real genotypes, with only two studies using both.
evidence: This is an inference from the literature review presented in Table 1.

claim: 10/12 papers with quantitative traits favor LMMs.
source: Similarly, 10/12 papers with quantitative traits favor LMMs, whereas 6/9 papers with case-control traits gave ties or mixed results—the only factor we do not explore in this work.
evidence: This is an inference from the literature review presented in Table 1.

claim: 6/9 papers with case-control traits gave ties or mixed results.
source: Similarly, 10/12 papers with quantitative traits favor LMMs, whereas 6/9 papers with case-control traits gave ties or mixed results—the only factor we do not explore in this work.
evidence: This is an inference from the literature review presented in Table 1.

claim: A large fraction (6/17) of previous evaluations did not measure power.
source: Additionally, although all previous evaluations measured type I error (or proxies such as genomic inflation factors Devlin and Roeder, 1999 or QQ plots), a large fraction (6/17) did not measure power (or proxies such as ROC curves), and only four used more than one number of PCs for PCA.
evidence: This is an inference from the literature review presented in Table 1.

claim: Only four previous studies used more than one number of PCs for PCA.
source: Additionally, although all previous evaluations measured type I error (or proxies such as genomic inflation factors Devlin and Roeder, 1999 or QQ plots), a large fraction (6/17) did not measure power (or proxies such as ROC curves), and only four used more than one number of PCs for PCA.
evidence: This is an inference from the literature review presented in Table 1.

claim: The admixture Large simulation has 1000 individuals.
source: The 'large' version (1000 individuals) illustrates asymptotic performance, while the 'small' simulation (100 individuals) illustrates model overfitting.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation design.

claim: The admixture Small simulation has 100 individuals.
source: The 'large' version (1000 individuals) illustrates asymptotic performance, while the 'small' simulation (100 individuals) illustrates model overfitting.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation design.

claim: The family simulation has admixed founders and draws a 20-generation random pedigree with assortative mating.
source: The 'family' simulation has admixed founders and draws a 20-generation random pedigree with assortative mating, resulting in a complex joint family and ancestry structure in the last generation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation design.

claim: Subpopulation tree simulations fit to real human datasets by design do not have family structure.
source: Last are subpopulation tree simulations (Figure 1F, I, L) fit to the kinship (Figure 1E, H and K) and MAF (Figure 1C) of each real human dataset, which by design do not have family structure.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation design.

claim: The FES model captures the rough inverse relationship between coefficient and minor allele frequency that arises under strong negative and balancing selection.
source: The FES model captures the rough inverse relationship between coefficient and minor allele frequency that arises under strong negative and balancing selection and has been observed in numerous diseases and other traits (Park et al., 2011; Zeng et al., 2018; Simons et al., 2018; O'Connor et al., 2019), so it is the focus of our results.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on the relationship between effect sizes and allele frequencies.

claim: The inverse relationship between coefficient and minor allele frequency has been observed in numerous diseases and other traits.
source: The FES model captures the rough inverse relationship between coefficient and minor allele frequency that arises under strong negative and balancing selection and has been observed in numerous diseases and other traits (Park et al., 2011; Zeng et al., 2018; Simons et al., 2018; O'Connor et al., 2019), so it is the focus of our results.
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The RC model draws coefficients independent of allele frequency, corresponding to neutral traits.
source: The RC model draws coefficients independent of allele frequency, corresponding to neutral traits (Zeng et al., 2018; Simons et al., 2018), which results in a wider effect size distribution that reduces association power and effective polygenicity compared to FES.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation design supported by citations.

claim: In the family simulation, LMM is conclusively superior to PCA, and the only calibrated model.
source: Thus, LMM is conclusively superior to PCA, and the only calibrated model, when there is family structure.
evidence: This is an inference from the results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Human Origins has the greatest number and diversity of subpopulations among the real datasets.
source: Human Origins has the greatest number and diversity of subpopulations.
evidence: This is supported by the dataset description in Table 2 and Figure 1.

claim: HGDP has the fewest individuals among real datasets.
source: HGDP has the fewest individuals among real datasets, but compared to Human Origins contains more loci and low-frequency variants.
evidence: This is supported by the dataset description in Table 2.

claim: HGDP contains more loci and low-frequency variants compared to Human Origins.
source: HGDP has the fewest individuals among real datasets, but compared to Human Origins contains more loci and low-frequency variants.
evidence: This is supported by the dataset description in Table 2 and Figure 1C.

claim: 1000 Genomes has the fewest subpopulations but largest number of individuals per subpopulation among the real datasets.
source: 1000 Genomes has the fewest subpopulations but largest number of individuals per subpopulation.
evidence: This is supported by the dataset description in Table 2.

claim: Subpopulation tree simulations feature non-uniform ancestral allele frequency distributions, which recapitulated some of the skew for smaller minor allele frequencies of the real datasets.
source: These tree simulations also feature non-uniform ancestral allele frequency distributions, which recapitulated some of the skew for smaller minor allele frequencies of the real datasets (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Subpopulation tree simulations do not recapitulate the large LMM advantage over PCA observed on the real data.
source: Overall, these subpopulation tree simulations do not recapitulate the large LMM advantage over PCA observed on the real data.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the results in Figures 5 and 4.

claim: The true rank of simulations is slightly underestimated by the Tracy-Widom test.
source: The true rank of our simulations is slightly underestimated (Table 2), but we confirm that the family simulation has the greatest rank, and real datasets have greater estimates than their respective subpopulation tree simulations, which confirms our hypothesis to some extent.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the estimated ranks in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A with the known simulation parameters in Table 2.

claim: The family simulation has the greatest kinship matrix rank estimate.
source: The true rank of our simulations is slightly underestimated (Table 2), but we confirm that the family simulation has the greatest rank, and real datasets have greater estimates than their respective subpopulation tree simulations, which confirms our hypothesis to some extent.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Real datasets have greater kinship matrix rank estimates than their respective subpopulation tree simulations.
source: The true rank of our simulations is slightly underestimated (Table 2), but we confirm that the family simulation has the greatest rank, and real datasets have greater estimates than their respective subpopulation tree simulations, which confirms our hypothesis to some extent.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Estimated kinship matrix ranks do not separate real datasets from tree simulations, as required to predict the observed PCA performance.
source: However, estimated ranks do not separate real datasets from tree simulations, as required to predict the observed PCA performance.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the rank estimates in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A with the PCA performance results.

claim: The family simulation has much greater variance explained by mid-rank eigenvalues compared to other datasets.
source: Comparing cumulative variance explained versus rank fraction across all eigenvalues, all datasets increase from their starting point almost linearly until they reach 1, except the family simulation has much greater variance explained by mid-rank eigenvalues (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no separation between real datasets (where PCA performed poorly) and subpopulation tree simulations (where PCA performed relatively well) in terms of their eigenvalues or kinship matrix rank estimates.
source: Overall, there is no separation between real datasets (where PCA performed poorly) and subpopulation tree simulations (where PCA performed relatively well) in terms of their eigenvalues or kinship matrix rank estimates.
evidence: This is an inference from the eigenvalue and rank analyses in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: More large local kinship is observed in the real datasets and the family simulation compared to the other simulations.
source: We observe more large local kinship in the real datasets and the family simulation compared to the other simulations (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Highly related individual pairs with kinship above the 4th degree relative threshold of 0.022 were identified in all real datasets.
source: In all real datasets, we identified highly related individual pairs with kinship above the 4th degree relative threshold of 0.022 (Manichaikul et al., 2010; Conomos et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Highly related pairs are vastly outnumbered by more distant pairs with evident non-zero local kinship in real datasets.
source: However, these highly related pairs are vastly outnumbered by more distant pairs with evident non-zero local kinship as compared to the extreme tree simulation values.
evidence: This is an inference from the results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Removing 4th degree relatives reduced sample sizes between 5% and 10% in real datasets.
source: To try to improve PCA performance, we followed the standard practice of removing 4th degree relatives, which reduced sample sizes between 5% and 10% (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by the results presented in Table 4.

claim: The removal of the small number of highly related individual pairs had a negligible effect on PCA performance.
source: Therefore, the removal of the small number of highly related individual pairs had a negligible effect in PCA performance, so the larger number of more distantly related pairs explain the poor PCA performance in the real datasets.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the results before (Figure 4) and after (Figure 7) removing 4th degree relatives.

claim: The larger number of more distantly related pairs explain the poor PCA performance in the real datasets.
source: Therefore, the removal of the small number of highly related individual pairs had a negligible effect in PCA performance, so the larger number of more distantly related pairs explain the poor PCA performance in the real datasets.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the results before (Figure 4) and after (Figure 7) removing 4th degree relatives.

claim: Environment simulations are the only cases where a significant, though small, advantage of LMM with PCs versus LMM without PCs is occasionally observed for both metrics.
source: These simulations are the only where we occasionally observed for both metrics a significant, though small, advantage of LMM with PCs versus LMM without PCs (Table 6).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparisons presented in Table 6.

claim: On RC traits with environment effects, PCA significantly outperforms LMM in the three real human datasets.
source: Additionally, on RC traits only, PCA significantly outperforms LMM in the three real human datasets (Table 6), the only cases in all of our evaluations where this is observed.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparisons presented in Table 6.

claim: LMM with labels is often more poorly calibrated than LMM or PCA without labels.
source: However, LMM with labels is often more poorly calibrated than LMM or PCA without labels, which may be since these numerous labels are inappropriately modeled as fixed rather than random effects.
evidence: This is an inference from the results shown in Figure 8 and Table 6.

claim: Addition of PCs to an LMM improves performance only marginally in the presence of environment effects.
source: Overall, we find that association studies with correlated environment and genetic effects remain a challenge for PCA and LMM, that addition of PCs to an LMM improves performance only marginally, and that if the environment effect is driven by geography or ethnicity then use of those labels greatly improves performance compared to using PCs.
evidence: This is an inference from the results shown in Figure 8 and Table 6.

claim: If the environment effect is driven by geography or ethnicity then use of those labels greatly improves performance compared to using PCs.
source: Overall, we find that association studies with correlated environment and genetic effects remain a challenge for PCA and LMM, that addition of PCs to an LMM improves performance only marginally, and that if the environment effect is driven by geography or ethnicity then use of those labels greatly improves performance compared to using PCs.
evidence: This is an inference from the results shown in Figure 8 and Table 6.

claim: LMM and PCA are closely related models.
source: LMM and PCA are closely related models (Astle and Balding, 2009; Janss et al., 2012; Hoffman and Dubé, 2013; Zhang and Pan, 2015), so similar performance is expected particularly under low-dimensional relatedness.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Including both PCs and kinship-parameterized random effects in an LMM is redundant because PCs are the eigenvectors of the same kinship matrix.
source: Our findings make sense since PCs are the eigenvectors of the same kinship matrix that parameterized random effects, so including both is redundant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mathematical relationship between PCs and the kinship matrix.

claim: LMM without PCs models environment effects nearly as well as with PCs.
source: However, we observe that LMM without PCs models environment effects nearly as well as with PCs (Figure 8), consistent with previous findings (Vilhjálmsson and Nordborg, 2013; Wang et al., 2022) and with environment inflating heritability estimates using LMM (Heckerman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 8 and citations to previous work.

claim: Including PCs to model environment effects yields limited power gains if at all, even in an LMM.
source: Overall, including PCs to model environment effects yields limited power gains if at all, even in an LMM, and is no replacement for more adequate modeling of environment whenever possible.
evidence: This is an inference from the results shown in Figure 8 and Table 6.

claim: Previous studies found that PCA was better calibrated than LMM for unusually differentiated markers.
source: Previous studies found that PCA was better calibrated than LMM for unusually differentiated markers (Price et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2014), which as simulated were an artificial scenario not based on a population genetics model, and are otherwise believed to be unusual (Sul and Eskin, 2013; Price et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Evaluations on real human data do not replicate the result that PCA is better calibrated than LMM for unusually differentiated markers.
source: Our evaluations on real human data, which contain such loci in relevant proportions if they exist, do not replicate that result.
evidence: This is an inference from the results on real data (Figures 4, 7, 8).

claim: Family relatedness strongly favors LMM, an advantage that probably outweighs the potential PCA benefit for unusually differentiated markers in real data.
source: Family relatedness strongly favors LMM, an advantage that probably outweighs this potential PCA benefit in real data.
evidence: This is an inference from the results showing strong LMM performance in family simulations and real data.

claim: PCA performed well in the admixture simulations (without families, both trait models), real human genotypes with RC traits, and the subpopulation tree simulations (both trait models).
source: PCA performed well in the admixture simulations (without families, both trait models), real human genotypes with RC traits, and the subpopulation tree simulations (both trait models).
evidence: This is a summary of the results from Figures 3, 4, 5, and Tables 3, 5.

claim: PCA performed poorly in the admixed family simulation (both trait models) and the real human genotypes with FES traits.
source: Conversely, PCA performed poorly in the admixed family simulation (both trait models) and the real human genotypes with FES traits.
evidence: This is a summary of the results from Figures 3, 4, and Tables 3, 5.

claim: PCA performs well in the admixture simulation because it is explicitly low-dimensional.
source: Thus, PCA performs well in the admixture simulation, which is explicitly low-dimensional (see Genotype simulation from the admixture model), and our subpopulation tree simulations, which are likely well approximated by a few dimensions despite the large number of subpopulations because there are few long branches.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the admixture simulation and PCA performance.

claim: Subpopulation tree simulations are likely well approximated by a few dimensions despite the large number of subpopulations because there are few long branches.
source: Thus, PCA performs well in the admixture simulation, which is explicitly low-dimensional (see Genotype simulation from the admixture model), and our subpopulation tree simulations, which are likely well approximated by a few dimensions despite the large number of subpopulations because there are few long branches.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the tree simulations and PCA performance.

claim: PCA performs poorly under family structure because its kinship matrix is high-dimensional.
source: Conversely, PCA performs poorly under family structure because its kinship matrix is high-dimensional (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinship matrix rank estimates and PCA performance.

claim: Kinship matrix rank estimated using the Tracy-Widom test did not fully predict the datasets that PCA performs well on.
source: Kinship matrix rank estimated using the Tracy-Widom test (Patterson et al., 2006) did not fully predict the datasets that PCA performs well on.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the rank estimates with PCA performance.

claim: Local kinship better explains why PCA performs poorly in real datasets than kinship matrix rank estimates.
source: In contrast, estimated local kinship finds considerable cryptic family relatedness in all real human datasets and better explains why PCA performs poorly there.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the local kinship results (Figure 6) with PCA performance.

claim: Hundreds of close relative pairs have been identified in 1000 Genomes.
source: Hundreds of close relative pairs have been identified in 1000 Genomes (Gazal et al., 2015; Al Khudhair et al., 2015; Fedorova et al., 2016; Schlauch et al., 2017), but their removal does not improve PCA performance sufficiently in our tests, so the larger number of more distantly related pairs are PCA's most serious obstacle in practice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Removal of close relative pairs does not improve PCA performance sufficiently.
source: Hundreds of close relative pairs have been identified in 1000 Genomes (Gazal et al., 2015; Al Khudhair et al., 2015; Fedorova et al., 2016; Schlauch et al., 2017), but their removal does not improve PCA performance sufficiently in our tests, so the larger number of more distantly related pairs are PCA's most serious obstacle in practice.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The larger number of more distantly related pairs are PCA's most serious obstacle in practice.
source: Hundreds of close relative pairs have been identified in 1000 Genomes (Gazal et al., 2015; Al Khudhair et al., 2015; Fedorova et al., 2016; Schlauch et al., 2017), but their removal does not improve PCA performance sufficiently in our tests, so the larger number of more distantly related pairs are PCA's most serious obstacle in practice.
evidence: This is an inference from the results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Distant relatives are expected to be numerous in any large human dataset.
source: Distant relatives are expected to be numerous in any large human dataset (Henn et al., 2012; Shchur and Nielsen, 2018; Loh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: FES trait tests show that family relatedness is more challenging when rarer variants have larger coefficients.
source: Our FES trait tests show that family relatedness is more challenging when rarer variants have larger coefficients.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing FES and RC trait results.

claim: The high relatedness dimensions induced by family relatedness is the key challenge for PCA association in modern datasets that is readily overcome by LMM.
source: Overall, the high relatedness dimensions induced by family relatedness is the key challenge for PCA association in modern datasets that is readily overcome by LMM.
evidence: This is an inference from all the results showing poor PCA performance in the presence of family relatedness.

claim: PCA is robust to large numbers of PCs, far beyond the optimal choice.
source: Our tests also found PCA robust to large numbers of PCs, far beyond the optimal choice, agreeing with previous anecdotal observations (Price et al., 2006; Kang et al., 2010), in contrast to using too few PCs for which there is a large performance penalty.
evidence: This is supported by the results in Figures 3-5 and citations to previous work.

claim: The exception to PCA robustness to large numbers of PCs was the small sample size simulation.
source: The exception was the small sample size simulation, where only small numbers of PCs performed well.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An LMM with a large number of covariates may have conservative p-values.
source: However, an LMM with a large number of covariates may have conservative p-values, as observed for LMM with large numbers of PCs, which is a weakness of the score test used by the LMM we evaluated that may be overcome with other statistical tests.
evidence: This is an inference from the results showing negative SRMSD_p for LMM with large r.

claim: The LOCO approach for estimating kinship matrices for LMMs prevents the test locus and loci in LD with it from being modeled by the random effect.
source: Similarly, the leave-one-chromosome-out (LOCO) approach for estimating kinship matrices for LMMs prevents the test locus and loci in LD with it from being modeled by the random effect as well, which is called 'proximal contamination' (Lippert et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the LOCO method supported by citations.

claim: LOCO kinship estimates continue to model family relatedness, thus maintaining their key advantage over PCA.
source: While LOCO kinship estimates vary for each chromosome, they continue to model family relatedness, thus maintaining their key advantage over PCA.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of LOCO kinship estimates.

claim: In this work, simulated genotypes do not have LD, and the real datasets were filtered to remove LD.
source: However, in this work, simulated genotypes do not have LD, and the real datasets were filtered to remove LD, so here there is no proximal contamination and LD confounding is minimized if present at all, so these evaluations may be considered the ideal situation where LD effects have been adjusted successfully, and in this setting LMM outperforms PCA.
evidence: This is a description of the study design.

claim: In the ideal situation where LD effects have been adjusted successfully, LMM outperforms PCA.
source: However, in this work, simulated genotypes do not have LD, and the real datasets were filtered to remove LD, so here there is no proximal contamination and LD confounding is minimized if present at all, so these evaluations may be considered the ideal situation where LD effects have been adjusted successfully, and in this setting LMM outperforms PCA.
evidence: This is an inference from the results showing LMM outperforming PCA in the absence of LD.

claim: The conclusions of this work are not expected to change with larger sample sizes.
source: However, our conclusions are not expected to change with larger sample sizes, as cryptic family relatedness will continue to be abundant in such data, if not increase in abundance, and thus give LMMs an advantage over PCA (Henn et al., 2012; Shchur and Nielsen, 2018; Loh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous work on the prevalence of distant relatives.

claim: Recent approaches have made LMMs more scalable and applicable to biobank-scale data.
source: However, recent approaches not tested in this work have made LMMs more scalable and applicable to biobank-scale data (Loh et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2018; Mbatchou et al., 2021), so one clear next step is carefully evaluating these approaches in simulations with larger sample sizes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent methodological papers.

claim: For BOLT-LMM, including PCs does not result in greater power but rather in reduced runtime.
source: A different benefit for including PCs were recently reported for BOLT-LMM, which does not result in greater power but rather in reduced runtime, a property that may be specific to its use of scalable algorithms such as conjugate gradient and variational Bayes (Loh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the BOLT-LMM paper.

claim: Rare variants can have a more pronounced structure than common variants.
source: Using simulations mimicking the UK Biobank, recent work has found that rare variants can have a more pronounced structure than common variants, and that modeling this rare variant structure (with either PCA and LMM) may better model environment confounding, reduce inflation in association studies, and ameliorate stratification in polygenic risk scores (Zaidi and Mathieson, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: Previous evaluations involving case-control traits tended to report PCA-LMM ties or mixed results.
source: Previous evaluations involving case-control traits tended to report PCA-LMM ties or mixed results, an observation potentially confounded by the use of low-dimensional simulations without family relatedness (Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the literature review presented in Table 1.

claim: Case-control ascertainment bias and imbalance appears to affect LMMs more severely.
source: An additional concern is case-control ascertainment bias and imbalance, which appears to affect LMMs more severely, although recent work appears to solve this problem (Yang et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The authors recommend LMM over PCA for association studies in general.
source: Overall, our results lead us to recommend LMM over PCA for association studies in general.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the overall results of the study.

claim: The large numbers of distant relatives expected of any real dataset all but ensures that PCA will perform poorly compared to LMM.
source: The large numbers of distant relatives expected of any real dataset all but ensures that PCA will perform poorly compared to LMM (Henn et al., 2012; Shchur and Nielsen, 2018; Loh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference from the results and citations to previous work on the prevalence of distant relatives.

claim: Related applications such as polygenic models may enjoy gains in power and accuracy by employing an LMM instead of PCA to model relatedness.
source: Our findings also suggest that related applications such as polygenic models may enjoy gains in power and accuracy by employing an LMM instead of PCA to model relatedness (Rakitsch et al., 2013; Qian et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of this study and citations to related work.

claim: PCA remains indispensable across population genetics, from visualizing population structure and performing quality control to its deep connection to admixture models.
source: PCA remains indispensable across population genetics, from visualizing population structure and performing quality control to its deep connection to admixture models, but the time has come to limit its use in association testing in favor of LMM or other, richer models capable of modeling all forms of relatedness.
evidence: This is a statement based on general knowledge of the field.
